title: Context Switch Rate Anomaly Detection (Linux)
exclusions: Detects sustained host-level changes in the system-wide Linux context-switch rate derived from the cumulative `cSwitches` counter. It does not identify the process or thread responsible, separate voluntary from involuntary switches, normalize by CPU count, prove scheduler saturation, cover containers independently of their host, or establish regulatory compliance. The primary SPL does not silently apply maintenance exclusions.
evidence: When deployed, retain the `linux_context_switch_rate_anomaly_15m` saved-search definition, alert history, and dashboard exports containing `host`, `window_start`, `window_end`, `min_context_switch_rate`, `avg_context_switch_rate`, `current_context_switch_rate`, `current_baseline_rate`, and `current_upper_bound`. These artifacts evidence configured monitoring and observed results, not production validation or root cause.

controlTest.positiveScenario: Create one-minute `vmstat` events for `host=cs-positive` with monotonically increasing numeric `cSwitches`. Supply at least 216 complete five-minute baseline buckets whose deltas equal 1,000 switches/second, followed by all three closed candidate buckets at 2,000 switches/second. The search must return one row with `observed_buckets=3`, `complete_buckets=3`, `anomalous_buckets=3`, and rates expressed in switches/second.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Use the same 1,000-switches/second baseline for `host=cs-negative`, but raise only the first candidate bucket to 2,000 switches/second and return the next two to 1,000. The search must return no row because `anomalous_buckets` is less than three. In a separate reset check, decrease `cSwitches` between adjacent samples; that interval must become null and must never be interpreted as a rate spike.

dataSources: `index=os sourcetype=vmstat source=vmstat` events from the `vmstat.sh` scripted event input in the Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833). Required event fields are `_time`, `host`, and numeric `cSwitches`. On Linux, the add-on collector obtains this cumulative count from `vmstat -s`; `os` is a deployment-selected event index.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833), deployed to Linux Universal Forwarders that execute `vmstat.sh` and to the Splunk tiers required for parsing and search-time knowledge.
spl:
index=os sourcetype=vmstat source=vmstat host=* earliest=-25h@m latest=-5m@m
| eval cSwitches=tonumber(cSwitches)
| where isnotnull(cSwitches)
| stats max(cSwitches) as cSwitches by host _time
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats current=f window=1 last(cSwitches) as previous_cswitches last(_time) as previous_time by host
| eval elapsed_seconds=_time-previous_time
| eval context_switch_delta=if(cSwitches>=previous_cswitches,cSwitches-previous_cswitches,null())
| eval context_switch_rate=if(elapsed_seconds>0 AND elapsed_seconds<=180,context_switch_delta/elapsed_seconds,null())
| where isnotnull(context_switch_rate)
| bin _time span=5m
| stats avg(context_switch_rate) as context_switch_rate count as rate_samples by host _time
| where rate_samples>=4
| sort 0 host _time
| streamstats current=f window=288 avg(context_switch_rate) as baseline_rate stdev(context_switch_rate) as baseline_stddev count as baseline_buckets by host
| where baseline_buckets>=216 AND isnotnull(baseline_stddev) AND baseline_rate>0
| eval upper_bound=baseline_rate+(3*baseline_stddev)
| eval anomalous=if(context_switch_rate>upper_bound AND context_switch_rate>=baseline_rate*1.5,1,0)
| eval candidate_start=relative_time(now(),"-20m@m"), candidate_end=relative_time(now(),"-5m@m")
| where _time>=candidate_start AND _time<candidate_end
| stats count as observed_buckets sum(anomalous) as anomalous_buckets min(rate_samples) as min_rate_samples min(_time) as window_start max(_time) as window_end min(context_switch_rate) as min_context_switch_rate avg(context_switch_rate) as avg_context_switch_rate latest(context_switch_rate) as current_context_switch_rate latest(baseline_rate) as current_baseline_rate latest(upper_bound) as current_upper_bound by host
| eval complete_buckets=observed_buckets
| where observed_buckets=3 AND complete_buckets=3 AND anomalous_buckets=3
| eval min_context_switch_rate=round(min_context_switch_rate,1), avg_context_switch_rate=round(avg_context_switch_rate,1), current_context_switch_rate=round(current_context_switch_rate,1), current_baseline_rate=round(current_baseline_rate,1), current_upper_bound=round(current_upper_bound,1)
| sort 0 -avg_context_switch_rate
description: Reports a Linux host only when each of the three most recent closed five-minute buckets has a context-switch rate above both its prior rolling baseline plus three sample standard deviations and 150 percent of that baseline. The search derives switches/second from adjacent `cSwitches` counter samples, rejects counter decreases and long collection gaps, and requires at least four valid rates per bucket.
value: A persistent departure from a host's own scheduling pattern can reveal thread storms, lock contention, interrupt-heavy work, or workload regressions before they become sustained latency. Requiring three complete anomalous buckets and both statistical and relative gates reduces pages from one short burst, while preserving the rate and baseline responders need for triage.
implementation: Deploy Splunkbase 833, enable its existing `vmstat.sh` event input at a 60-second interval, and verify that `cSwitches` is numeric and normally nondecreasing. Save the search with its explicit 25-hour window and run it every five minutes on bucket boundaries. Treat three sigma plus a 50-percent relative rise for 15 minutes as a tunable starting policy, not a Linux or Splunk vendor threshold.
visualization: Use a per-host line chart with `context_switch_rate`, `baseline_rate`, and `upper_bound` on one axis labelled `context switches/second`; a table of sustained anomalies with `min_rate_samples`; and drilldowns to CPU, run-queue, interrupt, process, deployment, and reboot data. Do not chart raw cumulative `cSwitches` as though it were a rate.
dataModelAcceleration: The add-on tags `sourcetype=vmstat` for the Performance model, but CIM Performance 6.4 defines no normalized context-switch counter or rate field. Do not substitute `cpu_load_percent` and do not claim an equivalent accelerated `tstats` search; the detection must retain source-specific `cSwitches` and calculate its delta over elapsed seconds.

knownFalsePositives:
1. **GCC, Clang, Maven, or Gradle parallel builds** — A sanctioned build fan-out can legitimately create many runnable threads. Correlate the same host and window with `sourcetype=ps`, the CI job identifier, CPU utilization, and service latency; suppress only the exact build window after the workload owner confirms it.

2. **Veeam, rsync, PostgreSQL, or Oracle maintenance jobs** — Backup compression, checksum workers, and database parallelism can change scheduling behavior on a fixed timetable. Match the anomaly to the scheduler and an approved change record; use a host-and-time-bounded exception rather than excluding the product permanently.

3. **systemd package maintenance and service restart waves** — `apt-daily`, `dnf-automatic`, initramfs generation, and restart fan-out can sustain an elevated rate. Confirm package-manager and change events, then expire the exception when the maintenance window closes.

4. **Kubernetes, Nomad, or Slurm batch placement** — A planned placement wave on a shared node may be healthy even though the host baseline is exceeded. Compare pod/job starts, run queue, CPU, and application SLOs; suppress the named job window or tune a separate host-class policy.

5. **Baseline warm-up after onboarding or workload migration** — A new host, CPU resize, kernel change, or permanent workload move can make the preceding 24 hours unrepresentative. Confirm the inventory/change record and withhold alerting until at least 216 complete baseline buckets exist; then review whether the baseline window or host class should change.

**Suppression mechanism:** the primary SPL has no hidden allow-list. If policy requires suppression, append a reviewed `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv` lookup keyed by exact `host`, `start_epoch`, and `end_epoch`, filter only currently active rows, and require owner, reason, ticket, and expiry. Never use wildcard or non-expiring entries.
reviewer: documentation review against Splunk and Linux primary sources; no production execution or SME sign-off
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and signal semantics

Use the supported Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) and confirm the selected release supports the deployment's Linux and Splunk versions. The Splunkbase listing currently identifies 10.2.0 as the default release and warns that upgrades from pre-6.0 layouts require testing because defaults and configuration files changed. Install the add-on on every Linux Universal Forwarder that runs the collector, on search heads that need its knowledge objects, and on the parsing tier required by the documented topology. The search role needs read access to the chosen operating-system event index; it does not need administrator rights.

The semantic distinction is essential. Linux `/proc/stat` exposes `ctxt` as a system-wide count accumulated since boot. The add-on's Linux `vmstat.sh` collector reads summary statistics and emits that count as `cSwitches`. It is not the native periodic `vmstat` column named `cs`; `vmstat(8)` defines `cs` as switches per second, but this sidecar does not receive that periodic column. Therefore, never average raw `cSwitches`. Derive `rate=(current_counter-previous_counter)/(current_time-previous_time)` and label the result `context switches/second`. A high host-level rate alone does not prove harmful scheduler pressure and cannot identify voluntary versus involuntary switches or the responsible task.

## Step 1 — Configure data collection and verify it

Create `Splunk_TA_nix/local/inputs.conf` in the deployment app and copy only the installed add-on's existing `vmstat.sh` stanza from `default/inputs.conf`; do not edit `default` or invent a replacement script path. A typical event-input override is:

```ini
[script://./bin/vmstat.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
sourcetype = vmstat
source = vmstat
index = os
```

The 60-second interval yields about 1,440 events per host per day. `os` is a local convention, so change the input and SPL together if another event index is approved. Deploy the app, restart the forwarder when required, and use `splunk btool inputs list --debug` on a representative host to verify that the local stanza wins. Search `index=os sourcetype=vmstat source=vmstat earliest=-10m` and require approximately one complete event per minute with numeric `_time`, `host`, and `cSwitches`. Do not use an ingest-reduction pipeline that removes this field, and do not point this event SPL at `vmstat_metric`.

On the same host, record two `vmstat -s` or `/proc/stat` observations around one collection interval and compare their counter delta with two adjacent Splunk events. Minor timing differences are expected; the counters must be of the same order and normally nondecreasing until reboot. Document the host timezone and forwarding lag if `_time` differs materially from collection time.

## Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Save the catalogue SPL as `linux_context_switch_rate_anomaly_15m`. Schedule it with cron `*/5 * * * *`. Keep its explicit `earliest=-25h@m latest=-5m@m`: the final five minutes are excluded because that bucket is still forming, while the extra history supplies a prior 24-hour rolling baseline and one preceding sample for the first delta.

`tonumber` rejects the add-on's documented `?` placeholder. `stats max(cSwitches) by host _time` collapses duplicate timestamps without summing a cumulative counter. Ascending `sort 0 host _time` is mandatory before both `streamstats` stages. The first `streamstats current=f window=1` copies only the preceding sample; a decrease is treated as a reboot/reset and produces null. Intervals longer than 180 seconds are dropped so a long collection outage is not presented as a current one-minute rate. Five-minute buckets average valid rates and require at least four, tolerating one missing sample without allowing a sparse point to stand for the bucket.

The second `streamstats current=f window=288` calculates each bucket's baseline from prior buckets only, preventing the current spike from directly diluting its own threshold. Require at least 216 complete buckets (18 hours) before evaluating. A candidate bucket must exceed `baseline_rate + 3*baseline_stddev` and be at least 150 percent of `baseline_rate`; then all three most recent closed buckets must pass. These are conservative operational starting rules, not vendor guarantees and not proof of a Gaussian distribution. Baseline web, database, build, and batch hosts separately. For strong daily seasonality, replace the rolling policy with a reviewed time-of-day baseline rather than weakening the sustained gate.

CIM Performance tags can help discover `vmstat` events, but CIM 6.4 has no normalized context-switch field. There is no honest accelerated `tstats` equivalent for this search. Trigger on result count greater than zero, notify per host, and throttle by `host` for 30 minutes.

## Step 3 — Validate counter, rate, and alert behavior

First, validate units with two adjacent real samples: manually compute `delta cSwitches / delta _time` and compare it with `context_switch_rate` before bucketing. Then test a reboot or synthetic counter decrease; the interval must be null, never a negative rate or huge positive wrap. Test a forwarding gap over 180 seconds; the spanning interval must be discarded and the affected bucket must fail the four-rate completeness gate if too few rates remain.

For the positive control, produce at least 216 complete baseline buckets at 1,000 switches/second and three closed candidate buckets at 2,000. Cumulative values must continue increasing; do not insert precomputed rates into `cSwitches`. The result must have three observed and anomalous buckets. For the negative control, make only one candidate bucket anomalous; no final row may survive. These are deterministic documentation tests. This review did not index fixtures or execute a saved search against a Splunk instance, so do not mark the UC verified on that basis.

Check collection continuity with `index=os sourcetype=vmstat earliest=-24h | timechart span=5m count by host limit=0`; investigate buckets materially below the configured cadence. Spot-check at least two hosts against `/proc/stat` or `vmstat -s`, including one recently rebooted host.

## Step 4 — Operationalize and investigate

Build a 24-hour line chart per host showing the derived rate, rolling baseline, and upper bound, plus a current-anomalies table containing all evidence fields. Keep the y-axis in `context switches/second`; never mix it with raw `cSwitches` or CPU percentage. Add drilldowns for the same host and time window to `sourcetype=cpu` (utilization, system time, I/O wait), `sourcetype=ps` or `pidstat -w` (task-level voluntary/involuntary switching), run queue and load, interrupts, deployments, reboots, and batch schedules.

The Linux operations runbook should first verify counter continuity and data completeness. Next decide whether service latency, run queue, system CPU, interrupts, or a recent process/deployment changed with the rate. Escalate to the workload owner before killing tasks, changing thread pools, pinning CPUs, or resizing a host. Review thresholds by host class after workload or CPU changes and review any exception lookup quarterly.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot and suppress safely

No `vmstat` events usually means the add-on is absent, the supplied input remains disabled, the script cannot execute, routing targets another index, or the role cannot search it. Events with no `cSwitches` require checking that the complete header-and-data event was indexed, the sourcetype is exactly `vmstat`, search-time knowledge is installed, and an Edge/Ingest Processor reduction did not remove the field. Rates that are null everywhere usually mean values are `?`, timestamps are duplicated, counters decrease at every sample, or gaps exceed 180 seconds. Implausibly huge rates require checking duplicate collectors, hostname reuse, timestamp quality, and whether events from two boots or systems were merged under one `host`. No alert despite visible spikes can be correct when fewer than 216 complete baseline buckets exist, any candidate bucket has fewer than four rates, the increase is below 150 percent, or fewer than three candidate buckets breach.

For approved maintenance, add a separate `linux_capacity_exceptions.csv` lookup with exact host, start and end epochs, owner, reason, and ticket. Filter only rows active for the result window and retain the unsuppressed result in alert history. Never use a permanent wildcard exclusion. The primary search intentionally contains no lookup because a catalogue cannot assert that a deployment-specific file exists.
grandmaExplanation: We watch how often a Linux server switches between pieces of work and compare it with that server's recent normal pattern. If the pace stays unusually high, the team can investigate before the extra juggling contributes to a slowdown.
